description.sr_latin: Kako da se dogovoriš za izlazak, predložiš aktivnosti, i organizuješ bleju.
description.en: How to make plans, suggest activities, and organize hangouts.

phrases.context: It's evening and you want to pull your partner off the couch and out into town.
phrases.notes: 'Hajde da' + present = 'let's'; 'izađemo' is from 'izaći' (to go out). The everyday way to float a plan.

phrases.context: The weather's nice and you'd rather stroll somewhere than sit; suggest it to whoever's with you.
phrases.notes: 'Prošetamo' = 'take a stroll'. An evening 'šetnja' along the river or through town is a real Serbian ritual.

phrases.context: You want to get someone out for a drink without committing to coffee, beer, or rakija yet.
phrases.notes: 'Popijemo' (perfective of 'piti') = down a drink; 'nešto' = 'something', left vague on purpose.

phrases.context: You're both staying in tonight and you want to pick a film or show to put on together.
phrases.notes: 'Gledamo' (from 'gledati') stays imperfective here — the watching is the activity, not a finished act.

phrases.en: Do you want to go out?
phrases.context: You're texting someone you like and want to ask, low-key, whether they're up for going out.
phrases.notes: 'Hoćeš da' + present = 'do you want to…'; works for a date or just hanging out, tone decides which.

phrases.en: Can we go to the cinema?
phrases.context: Something good is on the big screen and you want to nudge a friend into catching it with you.
phrases.notes: The verb of motion is dropped — 'možemo u bioskop' literally 'can we to the cinema'. 'U' + accusative marks the destination.

phrases.sr_latin: Ima jedan dobar restoran blizu, hoćeš da probamo?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Има један добар ресторан близу, хоћеш да пробамо?
phrases.en: There's a good place nearby, want to try it?
phrases.context: You've spotted a new restaurant near you and want to talk someone into eating there.
phrases.notes: 'Ima' here = 'there is'; 'jedan' softens it to 'a certain', not the number 'one'. 'Probamo' = 'let's try'.

phrases.context: It's late afternoon and you want to toss a colleague a quick, throwaway invite for one drink.
phrases.notes: 'Aj' is 'hajde' worn down to one syllable — peak-casual. 'Posle' takes the genitive, so 'posao' becomes 'posla'.

phrases.en: What are you doing this weekend?
phrases.context: It's Friday and you want to find out what a friend has going on before you propose anything.
phrases.notes: 'Za vikend' = 'for/over the weekend'. The classic opener before you suggest a plan.

phrases.sr_latin: Imaš li neke planove za vikend?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Имаш ли неке планове за викенд?
phrases.en: Do you have any plans for the weekend?
phrases.context: You want to ask a colleague about their weekend in a fuller, slightly more polished way.
phrases.notes: 'Li' after the verb forms a neutral yes/no question; 'planove' is accusative plural of 'plan' (the object).

phrases.context: A friend has just asked about your weekend and you want to shrug it off and bounce it back.
phrases.notes: 'Posebno' = 'special' in neuter, agreeing with 'ništa'. The standard low-key reply.

phrases.en: Shall we go somewhere this weekend?
phrases.context: You're itching to get out of town and want to pitch a vague weekend trip to your partner.
phrases.notes: Present tense 'idemo' here reads as a proposal — 'shall we go'. 'Negde' = 'somewhere', left open.

phrases.context: You want to ask a friend over to do absolutely nothing in particular at yours tonight.
phrases.notes: 'Bleja' is from 'blejati' (to bleat, like a sheep) — now the go-to slang for lazing around. 'Kod mene' = 'at my place' (gen).

phrases.context: You want to tell a whole group of friends to come over and just relax at yours.
phrases.notes: 'Dođite' is the plural/formal imperative of 'doći'; 'dođi' for one person. 'Chill' is borrowed straight from English.

phrases.context: Someone asks what the plan is and you want to say there isn't one — being together is enough.
phrases.notes: 'Blejimo' (from 'blejati') = 'we hang out / do nothing'. 'Samo da' = 'just to', framing it as the whole plan.

phrases.context: A friend just suggested a plan and you want to say yes to it in a single, eager word.
phrases.notes: Literally '(it) can', from 'moći', but used as all-purpose 'okay / sure / deal'. One of the most useful words you'll learn.

phrases.context: You've both landed on a plan and you want to lock it in with a casual 'done'.
phrases.notes: 'Važi' (from 'važiti', to hold/apply) = 'OK / deal'; 'dogovoreno' = 'agreed'. You'll hear 'važi' constantly.

phrases.context: Plans are set for something you're genuinely excited about and you want to show it.
phrases.notes: Literally 'I barely wait' — 'jedva' = 'barely', so together it's 'I can hardly wait'.

phrases.context: The meeting spot is settled and you want to wrap the chat with an upbeat confirmation.
phrases.notes: 'Vidimo se' = 'we see each other / see you'; the reflexive 'se' makes it mutual. 'Tamo' = 'there'.

phrases.sr_latin: Ne mogu danas, jel' može sutra?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Не могу данас, јел' може сутра?
phrases.en: I can't today, how about tomorrow?
phrases.context: You can't make it today but you still want to see the person, so offer another day.
phrases.notes: 'Ne mogu' = 'I can't' (1sg of 'moći'). 'Jel' može' = 'is it OK', a colloquial spoken 'da li je'.

phrases.en: It'll have to be another time.
phrases.context: You can't join and want to bow out gently without proposing a specific replacement day.
phrases.notes: 'Moraće' = future of 'morati' (will have to). 'Drugi put' = 'another time', literally 'a second time'.

phrases.context: You're worn out and want to honestly beg off and tell a friend you're not leaving the house.
phrases.notes: 'Umoran' = tired (masculine); 'umorna' if you're a woman. 'Kući' (dative) = 'at home / homeward'.

variations.en: I can't be bothered to go out.

phrases.en: What are you doing? / What's up?
phrases.context: You message a friend out of the blue to open a chat and see if they're around.
phrases.notes: 'Radiš' = 'you do' (from 'raditi'). Often just a conversation-opener, not a literal question.

phrases.en: Where are you? / Hey, what's up?
phrases.context: You're trying to find a friend in a crowd, or just tossing them a casual hello.
phrases.notes: 'Si' = 'you are' (2sg of 'biti'). As a greeting it's like 'hey there' and expects no real location.

phrases.context: Before you suggest anything, you want to check whether someone's actually open this evening.
phrases.notes: 'Jesi' is the emphatic 'are you' (from 'biti'). 'Slobodan' = free (masculine); 'slobodna' for a woman.

phrases.context: A plan is set but no hour was named, so you want to pin down when exactly to meet.
phrases.notes: 'Koliko' = 'how much/many'; 'sati' is the genitive plural of 'sat' (hour) after a quantity word.

phrases.context: You want to propose a concrete hour to settle the meeting time without sounding rigid.
phrases.notes: 'Recimo' = 'let's say' (1pl imperative of 'reći'). Heads up: 'u osam' often means 8:15–8:30 in practice.

phrases.en: Running a bit late, wait for me.
phrases.context: You're supposed to be there already and want to tell whoever's waiting to hold on.
phrases.notes: 'Sačekaj' = 'wait a bit' (imperative of 'sačekati'). 'Malo' = 'a little' — could mean 5 minutes or 30.

phrases.context: The time is agreed but not the spot, so you want to ask where to actually meet up.
phrases.notes: 'Da se nađemo' = 'should we meet'; the reflexive 'se' makes 'naći' (to find) into 'find each other'.

phrases.context: A friend is dragging their feet about coming and you want to talk them into it.
phrases.notes: 'Biće' = 'it will be' (future of 'biti'). 'Bre' comes from Turkish — an emphatic 'man / dude', deeply Serbian.

phrases.en: What are you waiting for? Let's go!
phrases.context: Someone's overthinking it and you want to snap them into just getting up and leaving.
phrases.notes: 'Čekaš' = 'you wait' (from 'čekati'); 'idemo' = 'we go / let's go', the all-purpose 'let's move'.

phrases.en: Oh come on, what's stopping you.
phrases.context: A friend keeps hesitating and you want to wave off their excuses with mock exasperation.
phrases.notes: 'Ma' before 'hajde' adds an insistent, fed-up tone. 'Šta ti fali' = 'what's wrong with you / what's missing'.

phrases.context: Everything's been agreed and you want to close the conversation cleanly and definitively.
phrases.notes: 'Onda' = 'then'; 'dogovoreno' = 'agreed/settled', a past passive form used as a one-word 'it's a deal'.

phrases.en: I'll text you when I leave.
phrases.context: You want to tell a friend you'll send word the moment you're actually heading out.
phrases.notes: 'Javim' (from 'javiti') = 'I'll let you know'; 'ti' is dative 'to you'. Present tense reads as future here.

phrases.context: Someone's heading to meet you and you want to ask them to ping you once they get there.
phrases.notes: 'Javi' = 'let me know' (imperative of 'javiti'); 'stigneš' = 'you arrive' (from 'stići').

phrases.context: You've got plans to meet and want to sign off the chat with a casual goodbye.
phrases.notes: 'Vidimo se' = 'we see each other'; the reflexive 'se' makes it 'see you'. The default casual sign-off.

variations.en: Talk later! / We'll be in touch!
